abstract: Inverse kinematics (IK) converts end-effector pose commands into joint motion, and many vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely on it to act on a given arm and to transfer across embodiments. Precise IK remains laborious: redundancy and singularities complicate the inverse mapping, execution depends on hand-tuned controllers, and training data on physical robots are costly to collect. We present PolicyIK, a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning policy for high-precision IK. It updates joint-position references from pose feedback and observes its accumulated reference relative to the measured joints, so it can retain the offset that the position controller needs at rest. Two-scale pose errors with an error-dependent action gain resolve millimeter residuals while preserving large motions. Progress and dwell rewards teach it to both reach the tolerance and stay within it. In simulation, a single attempt by the trained PPO policy keeps the mean errors over the final second within 1 mm and $0.2^{\circ}$ on 93.5% of held-out tasks, and a deployment protocol raises success to 98.9%. When trained directly on a physical arm with an off-policy RL learner, PolicyIK achieves higher reaching and holding success than all four classical IK controllers under the same time budgets. In simulated pick-and-place, PolicyIK executes the end-effector commands of the $\pi_{0.5}$ VLA policy with 95.7% success. These results show that reinforcement learning can provide high-precision inverse kinematics for robot arms. Code is available at https://github.com/Tinaliu0123/PolicyIK.

sections.body: The introduction argues that vision-language-action and generalist policies often output end-effector poses and depend on inverse kinematics to turn them into joint motion, so IK accuracy carries over to every such policy. Precise IK is difficult because of redundancy and singularities, robot-specific execution effects such as gravity and finite gains, and the cost of collecting physical training data. The paper proposes PolicyIK, a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning policy that updates joint-position references from pose feedback. It reports reaching and holding within 1 mm and 0.2°, direct training on two physical arms, and 95.7% success executing pi0.5 commands in simulated pick-and-place.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Policies that output end-effector poses inherit inverse kinematics accuracy, and precise inverse kinematics is hard to build.

sections.body: Related work covers classical IK methods, which are usually tuned per robot, and learned IK models that rely on numerical refinement for high accuracy. Prior reinforcement learning controllers report position goals or full-pose tracking with errors from millimeters to centimeters. One hybrid pairs a learned policy with damped least squares for the final correction and reaches sub-millimeter accuracy in kinematic simulation. The section also covers residual and integrating methods that compensate execution error. PolicyIK differs by learning closed-loop IK from interaction, observing the accumulated reference, and avoiding a numerical IK solver.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior learned reaching controllers reach millimeter to centimeter accuracy, and sub-millimeter results need a classical solver.

sections.body: The section formulates closed-loop pose regulation as a goal-conditioned Markov decision process for a 7-DoF arm. The state contains measured joint positions and velocities, the previous joint reference, and the previous action. The action is an increment to the joint reference, which a fixed-gain position controller tracks. The sparse reward is 1 when the position error is at most 1 mm and the rotation error is at most 0.2°. Evaluation is strict: the mean errors over the final 30 steps, which is 1 s, must meet these tolerances. Coarse diagnostics relax them to 1 cm and 2°, and containment requires the tolerance at every step of the final window.
sections.heading: Problem Formulation
sections.headline: Success is defined as mean errors over the final second within 1 mm and 0.2°, posed as goal-conditioned reinforcement learning.

sections.body: PolicyIK adds a scaled policy action to a joint reference that the position controller tracks, so a zero action keeps the offset the arm needs at rest. The observation includes the offset between reference and measured joints. Two pose-error channels, at 1 cm and 0.5 mm scales, let the policy perceive millimeter residuals. An error-dependent gain keeps the full step while error is large and shrinks it near the goal. The reward adds a progress term for each new best tolerance-normalized error and a dwell term paid at every step inside tolerance. For physical training, the section uses FlashSAC with hindsight relabeling, a latent-alignment critic, near-goal sampling, and a reverse curriculum.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: The method accumulates actions into a joint reference, scales them by error, and rewards each new best error and every step within tolerance.

sections.body: The simulation evaluates a fixed-base 7-DoF OpenArm on 4,120 start-goal pairs, with 160-step attempts and results averaged over three training seeds. A single PolicyIK attempt reaches 93.49 ± 0.20% strict success, with median errors of 0.25 mm and 0.04°. With the deployment protocol, strict success is 98.92 ± 0.23%. Damped least squares, resolved-rate quadratic programming, and a kinematic model-predictive controller reach 50.41%, 56.21%, and 56.33% strict success. Ablations show that removing command-state feedback lowers strict success by 9.2 points. In simulated pick-and-place with pi0.5 commands on ten LIBERO-Object tasks, PolicyIK reaches 95.7% success.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: In simulation, one attempt reaches 93.5% strict success, rising to 98.9% with the deployment protocol.

sections.body: The conclusion restates three design choices: reference accumulation with command-state feedback, two-scale pose errors with an error-dependent gain, and progress and dwell rewards. It says the ablations show that each design mainly raises terminal precision, so precise IK training should target the terminal phase. It reports that a single simulated attempt meets the tolerance on far more held-out tasks than tuned classical controllers. It states that training on a physical arm, using a reverse curriculum and near-goal sampling, yields a policy that reaches and holds more tasks than all four classical baselines. It also reports pick-and-place commands from pi0.5 without task-specific training.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Hardware training with the same terminal-phase design reaches and holds more tasks than all four classical controllers.

sections.body: Appendix A gives the simulation controller, an implicit PD with stiffness 80 and damping 4, a 54-dimensional observation, an action scale of 0.0625, and the data splits. Appendix B gives the PPO settings, reward weights, and an average of the last 20 checkpoints. Appendix C defines the containment metric and the deployment protocol, which uses an error-corrected goal and up to eight transient-goal attempts. Appendices D and E describe tuning of the simulation baselines. Appendix J reports that simulation-trained and hardware-trained policies each achieve 60/60 successes on standard reaching and on large rotations on an xArm7.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists simulation setup, reward and training settings, deployment protocol, baseline tuning, hardware controller settings, and xArm7 results.
